title: Positional Encoding
oneLineScope: Why a permutation-equivariant model needs order injected, and how (sinusoidal vs. learned).
prose:
Here is a fact about the attention operation you just met that is easy to miss and impossible to ignore once seen: it does not know the order of the tokens. Look again at \(\operatorname{softmax}(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k})\,V\). Each output row is a weighted sum over the value rows, and the weights come from dot products between query and key rows. A sum does not care about the order of its terms. If you permuted the rows of the input \(X\) — shuffled the tokens — the set of query/key/value vectors would be exactly the same set, the same pairwise dot products would be computed, and the outputs would simply come out in the correspondingly permuted order. The function is permutation-equivariant: permute the input and the output permutes the same way, but nothing about the content of any output vector changes. To the mechanism, a sentence is a bag.

That is fatal for language. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” are the same multiset of tokens; an order-blind model assigns them identical representations and cannot tell the headline from the tragedy. Recurrent networks never had this problem — they consumed tokens one at a time, so position was implicit in the timestep. Attention bought parallelism and direct long-range access by throwing away the sequential scan, and the order information went out with it. It has to be put back by hand. The fix is direct: before the first attention layer, add a position-dependent vector to each token's embedding, so that two copies of the same word sitting at different positions enter the network as different vectors.

Add, do not concatenate

Let \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\) be the token-embedding matrix — row \(i\) is the embedding of the \(i\)-th token, width \(d_{\text{model}}\). Positional encoding supplies a second matrix \(PE \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\) of the same shape, whose row \(i\) depends only on the position \(i\) and not on which token sits there. The block input is their element-wise sum:

\[ X = E + PE, \qquad X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}} \]

The choice to add rather than concatenate is worth a sentence, because it surprises people. Concatenating would cost width — \(d_{\text{model}}\) channels for content plus extra channels for position — and would wall the two off from each other. Adding keeps the width at \(d_{\text{model}}\) and lets the very first learned projection \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) read out whatever linear combination of content-plus-position it finds useful; because the projection is learned, it can carve out directions of the space that behave as positional and others that behave as lexical without our partitioning them in advance. The two signals share one residual stream and the optimizer sorts out the bookkeeping.

The sinusoidal encoding

Vaswani et al. define \(PE\) with a bank of sines and cosines. Index the position by \(pos \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}\) and the width by \(i \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d_{\text{model}}/2 - 1\}\); each pair of adjacent channels \((2i, 2i{+}1)\) gets a sine and a cosine of the same frequency:

\[ PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left( \frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d_{\text{model}}}} \right), \qquad PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left( \frac{pos}{10000^{\,2i/d_{\text{model}}}} \right) \]

Read the denominator as setting an angular frequency that decreases as the channel index \(i\) rises. At \(i = 0\) the wavelength is \(2\pi\); at the top channel it is \(2\pi \cdot 10000\). So as you sweep across the width \(d_{\text{model}}\) of one position's encoding, you are reading off the same position written in a geometric progression of wavelengths, from rapid oscillation in the low channels to a slow sweep in the high ones. It is, in effect, a multi-resolution clock — exactly the spirit of a positional number system, where each digit ticks at its own rate, but here the “digits” are continuous sinusoids. The construction is fixed: there are no learned parameters in \(PE\) at all.

Why this baroque choice rather than, say, writing the integer \(pos\) into one channel? The paper gives two reasons. First and central: for any fixed offset \(k\), the encoding of position \(pos+k\) is a linear function of the encoding of position \(pos\). This is just the angle-addition identity — \(\sin(\theta + \phi)\) and \(\cos(\theta+\phi)\) are fixed linear combinations of \(\sin\theta, \cos\theta\) once \(\phi\) is fixed — so within each frequency band, shifting position by \(k\) is multiplication by a \(2 \times 2\) rotation matrix whose angle is \(k\) times that band's angular frequency, depending on \(k\) but not on \(pos\). Think of each frequency band as a clock hand: advancing the position by a fixed \(k\) rotates every hand by its own fixed angle, the same rotation no matter where in the sequence you start. The consequence is the one that matters for attention: a head can implement “attend to the token three back” as a single fixed linear operation on the encodings, the same everywhere in the sequence. The model can learn to attend by relative position, which is what most syntactic relations actually care about. Second, and more speculative, the authors suggest the smooth fixed form might let the model extrapolate to sequences longer than any seen in training, since the function is defined for every \(pos\), not just the trained range.

The learned alternative, and the trade

There is a blunter option that GPT and BERT both took: make \(PE\) a trainable lookup table — one learned vector of width \(d_{\text{model}}\) per position, up to a fixed maximum length, optimized by gradient descent like any other parameter. No sinusoids, no structure imposed; the model simply learns whatever per-position vectors lower the loss. It is conceptually simpler and gives the model maximal freedom, at two costs: it adds \(n_{\max} \cdot d_{\text{model}}\) parameters, and — decisively — it has no value at all for any position beyond the maximum length it was trained on, because those table entries were never learned. The fixed sinusoid is at least defined there.

The honest punchline, which the reader should hold onto, is that Vaswani et al. tried both and reported them performing nearly identically on their translation task; they chose the sinusoidal version mainly for the extrapolation hope. So the contrast is real but the stakes, empirically, were modest:

 Sinusoidal (fixed)Learned (lookup table)
Parametersnone\(n_{\max} \cdot d_{\text{model}}\)
Relative-position structurebuilt in (linear shift)must be learned, if at all
Beyond trained lengthstill defined; may extrapolateundefined — hard cap at \(n_{\max}\)
Flexibilityshape is fixed in advancefree to fit the data
Used byoriginal TransformerGPT, BERT

Either way the deeper point stands: order is not native to attention, so it is supplied as an additive signal at the input, and the design space of how to supply it is one the field has kept reopening ever since.

Where it connects

This node and multi-head attention are the two pieces the prior scaled dot-product attention node left dangling: attention gives you content-based mixing but no order, and positional encoding repairs exactly that gap before the first layer. With both in hand, the next node assembles them into the transformer block — attention and a feed-forward layer, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization — the repeating unit that, stacked \(L\) deep on top of these position-aware embeddings, is the whole architecture.

A plus sign between them denotes element-wise addition, producing the block input matrix X of shape n by d_model on the right. A note marks that addition keeps the width at d_model and that PE depends only on position, not on the token.

diagrams.caption: The sinusoidal pattern as a position-by-dimension grid: low channels oscillate fast, high channels slow.
diagrams.altText: A grid whose vertical axis is position (pos 0 at top increasing downward) and whose horizontal axis is the embedding dimension (channel 0 on the left increasing rightward). Each column is a sinusoid of a fixed frequency; the leftmost columns oscillate rapidly down the position axis and the frequency decreases smoothly toward the right, so the rightmost columns sweep slowly. The banding makes a geometric progression of wavelengths visible. A note records that for any fixed offset k, PE(pos plus k) is a linear function of PE(pos), so relative position is a fixed linear shift.

bibliography.citation: Vaswani, A., et al. (2017). "Attention Is All You Need." NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The defining source. §3.5 gives the sinusoidal formulas verbatim, states the relative-position linearity and the extrapolation rationale, and reports that learned positional embeddings performed nearly identically (Table 3, row E). A few paragraphs; read it for the exact frequencies and the design justification.

bibliography.citation: Alammar, J. "The Illustrated Transformer" (positional encoding section).
bibliography.annotation: The clearest first look: it visualizes the position-by-dimension matrix as a banded heat map, which is the fastest way to see the geometric progression of frequencies. Start here if the sin/cos formulas do not immediately read as a multi-resolution clock.

bibliography.citation: Kazemnejad, A. "Transformer Architecture: The Positional Encoding."
bibliography.annotation: The careful derivation that fills in why the sinusoids work: it works out the 2x2 rotation matrix realizing a shift by k and shows explicitly that PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos). Go here for the relative-position argument in full, with the algebra the paper compresses to a sentence.

expansion: Deeper treatment the prose deliberately omits, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) the explicit 2x2 rotation matrix M_k with cos(k w_i)/sin(k w_i) entries that realizes the shift-by-k linearity within each frequency band, and the proof that it is independent of pos (Kazemnejad; Vaswani §3.5); (2) the precise wavelength range 2*pi to 2*pi*10000 and why 10000 was chosen as the base; (3) the empirical comparison to learned embeddings in Vaswani Table 3 (row E) and what 'nearly identical' meant numerically on their EN-DE task; (4) a forward pointer to relative-position and rotary schemes as the lineage that grew from the relative-position observation — name only, since they postdate this tutorial's scope and have no source in this bibliography. Cite each claim to its source section; do not introduce results from outside the bibliography.
